How DARPA Challenged Teams to Bring Robots Into Disaster Triage
description: On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City . They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money. The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge , which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events , such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes. Teams spent years designing systems where autonomous ground robots and drones could help first responders find mock victims and decide the best way to care for them. “Triage is all about resources,” says Jeremy Pamplin , who managed the challenge for DARPA. Pamplin is a critical care physician and retired colonel who spent 28 years in the U.S. Army. In mass casualty events, medics race to assess trauma with finite resources and limited time. Some victims need urgent help that medics can provide immediately, like tourniquets to halt bleeding. Some need evacuation and surgery. Others don’t need immediate help—either because their wounds are minimal enough, or because they’re so severe that a medic’s attention is better served elsewhere. Medics must prioritize who gets what care, but the line between each of these scenarios can be murky amid the rubble, frenzy, and heat of the moment. It’s a difficult problem, and so the technologies developed in this competition could help real-world decisionmaking, says Gabriela Garcia Dolagaray , assistant medical director for emergency preparedness at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. “Finding people can sometimes just be dangerous,” she says, “and getting a robust number of people to go out and search in a disaster area will take time.” Trauma Technologies and the DARPA Triage Challenge The Triage Challenge is the latest in a long DARPA legacy of running grand challenges to incentivize proof-of-concept development of important technologies. This particular challenge began as a program to quickly detect signs of trauma. DARPA imagined not only that drones and robots could find casualties, but that machine learning algorithms could assist in triage—which, at its core, is the process of assessing injuries and prioritizing care in a medical emergency. Pamplin took over the competition in May 2025. “I have friends that still wake up in the middle of the night with these types of recollections and wondering if they did the right thing in the moment during a mass casualty incident,” Pamplin says. “That moves me. I would very much like to eliminate that uncertainty for them to the extent possible with this type of technology.” He used his experience to make the competition increasingly elaborate and realistic. Year one featured a simulated convoy attack, and human participants sat in protective enclosures to avoid incidental run-ins with robots. In year two, when Pamplin took over the challenge, his team incorporated a full-size airplane fuselage to simulate a plane crash with dozens of victims. Organizers learned to recreate the physical environment of a disaster, and also the physical signs of injuries, like warm blood. Pamplin’s team visited a slaughterhouse with thermal cameras to study the temperature of blood spilling onto the ground. In the competition, they mimic that effect by heating water in a coffee pot and pouring it beside the body. This lets teams detect bleeding even at night. A man performs a simulated triage as part of DARPA’s Triage Challenge finals. The program was designed to see how robots could assist in making triage decisions during an emergency. Paul Flacks/DARPA “They always are throwing additional challenging things at us that you wouldn’t expect,” says Sam Colachis , a biomedical engineer at Battelle, an applied science and technology nonprofit in Columbus Ohio who led the organization’s DART team —short for “Drone-Assisted Rapid Triage”—in the competition. The tactics required for successful triage are inherently multidisciplinary, says Derek Paley , a professor of aerospace engineering leading the University of Maryland’s team, RoboScout . Before 2022, Paley felt confident in his lab’s skills with autonomous navigation and algorithms, but he knew little about trauma medicine. “I didn’t even know what triage was,” he says. Paley recruited colleagues in emergency medicine to help design his team’s approach and shape their tech. Before the Triage Challenge began, they felt like an underdog. “We kind of have a chip on our shoulder because we think we can play on the same field as these other teams…who’ve done grand challenges before,” Paley told Spectrum before the competition. They finished third in the first year of competition and second last year. Each year’s competition began with four smaller trials that tested specific components of a robotic system. Teams first released their robots to locate as many casualties (a mix of live actors and manikins ) as possible in 15 minutes. Next, they spent five minutes triaging injuries. Another trial presented teams with a fixed number of casualties in known locations to test how they assess trauma. Then, teams had ten minutes to collect vitals like pulse and breathing rate remotely from a few meters away. The top four teams moved into a semi-final where their robots worked with two human medics in simulated emergencies. And the two teams who performed best in four human-machine runs then moved to a 25-minute championship run. Robots, Drones, and Autonomous Triage When the teams arrived at Disaster City, they knew very little about the details of what awaited them. One self-funded team of college students from Delhi Technological University flew from India with 22 checked bags, each containing disembodied drones and wheeled robots they had handbuilt. Their team, Unmanned Aerial Systems , learned in the two prior years of the contest to simply expect the unexpected—from DARPA and their own systems. Upon arrival this year, they unzipped their luggage to find broken motors and chassis, camera parts, and missing screws. “We’re still trying to assemble everything before the competition,” Nishant Chandna calmly told IEEE Spectrum a couple days before the challenge. “It’s just part of it.” Most teams in the challenge designed systems with a mix of ground robots and aerial drones. The student team from India built drones and wheeled robots to search for mock victims with onboard cameras and lidar. But wheeled robots are problematic. They are more stable, cheaper, and easier to control than legged robots, but they struggle with stairs, entryways, and rough terrain littered with rubble. “We really needed a platform that could traverse those obstacles pretty easily,” says Eric Eaton , a machine learning scientist who led the University of Pennsylvania’s team, which began with drones and wheeled robots before expanding their fleet with four-legged Spot robots from Boston Dynamics that make it up stairs. Paley’s RoboScout team opted for a strategy that involved sensing the scene from the ground. Their “dogs,” which were also Spot robots, listen for screaming victims, and help in one of the most difficult challenges in autonomous triage: quickly sensing vitals from with thermal cameras and radar. Millimeter-wave radar can detect the subtle movement of a pulse, and thermal cameras can measure breathing rates based on how breathing changes the temperature around a mouth and nose. Battelle’s team had relied entirely on drones, even for measuring vital signs. Colachis says his team fuses inputs from multiple sensors including thermal, radar, and visual to calculate vitals. The team became almost notorious for their commitment to drones. “They keep threatening to bring a ground robot,” says RoboScout’s Paley, “but they always show up with drones.” For the first two years of the competition, it worked—Battelle won the first two rounds of the competition. Members of the University of Maryland’s RoboScout team (on right) celebrate a successful run during the DARPA Triage Challenge finals. Paul Flacks/DARPA RoboScout Wins DARPA Triage Grand Prize During the final, organizers cast more than 500 actors to simulate casualties throughout the week. DARPA chose these actors to make obstacles like sensing vitals more realistic than previous years. Some were college students instructed to increase their heart and breathing rate on exercise bikes to simulate shock. Endurance athletes were instructed to lower their heart rates, simulating other injuries like airway failures. In the military base simulation, soldiers were running around a compound with alarms blaring. “Some of the explosions caused some of the medics to actually react to it,” Pamplin says, and “pull people to the ground so they didn’t get hit.” Battelle did finally show up with a ground robot to help with measuring vitals remotely. But this time, the twice-champ finished second. The winner of DARPA’s Triage Challenge grand prize was the RoboScout team from the University of Maryland. The grand prize earned them $1.5 million. After a perilous start slowed by software errors relating to the competition’s timer and Wi-Fi RoboScout rallied back through the final human-machine teaming portion. “We got hot at the right time,” Paley says. “It was pretty surreal.” Other teams performed well despite having to improvise through engineering hiccups. Carnegie Mellon’s team, Chiron, struggled with a GPS error. After fixing it, they raced back and nearly made the final. The student team from Delhi didn’t meet a threshold for autonomous control in the competition, but they did earn the highest score in one sub-competition, winning $300,000. “It’s an incredibly exciting challenge,” says Peter Fischer, trauma medical director with Washington Regional Medical Center in Fayetteville, Arkansas. “We struggle, especially with mass casualty incidents, in determining who the sickest patients are. In trauma, especially, you have to make sure that you triage these patients appropriately, so the sickest ones not only get the care the fastest, but get to the right place at the right time.” Fischer was intrigued by a non-robotic branch of the competition, where two new teams excelled in predicting urgent care with the help of AI agents. He imagines these advances in robotics and algorithms could connect with additional data from hospitals. Triage algorithms could suggest where to take them to avoid overloading specific hospitals, he says, “That’s where we can really start to make a big difference.” Although the competition has ended, the work continues. Several participants told IEEE Spectrum they plan to bring their teams’ AI algorithms elsewhere, such as hospital trauma bays, regional medical emergencies, and chemical weapon response. For his part, DARPA’s Pamplin was most eager to compare performance to human medics without robots. A human-only team located 50 percent of casualties on average in daytime simulations; when paired with medics on one run of the same course, Maryland’s robots found every one. “That was the first time we’ve ever seen that,” he says. In the championship run, humans provided life-saving interventions to 25 percent of the mock casualties who needed them—RoboScout treated 74 percent. “That’s a couple lives,” Pamplin says. “That’s a couple humans that didn’t die that day.”
